analysis.one_liner: Suspended rent payments for tenants in federally assisted housing during the coronavirus emergency, with federal reimbursement to landlords.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on March 23, 2020 and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have suspended rent obligations for tenants living in federally assisted housing—public housing, Section 8 units, and a range of other subsidized housing—for the rest of the COVID-19 emergency plus six months. Tenants could not be evicted, fined, or billed for that rent, and it could not hurt their credit. Landlords and public housing agencies would have been paid back in full by the federal government, including extra pandemic-related costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants in federally assisted housing—public housing residents, Section 8 voucher households, and residents of other subsidized buildings—would have owed no rent during the emergency, faced no eviction or debt for nonpayment, and kept clean credit. Owners of assisted housing and public housing agencies would also benefit, because the bill authorized federal appropriations to reimburse them fully for all suspended rent plus added emergency costs.

how_it_helps.text: Tenants in assisted housing would owe no rent from enactment until six months after the COVID-19 emergency declaration ended.
Nonpayment could not be grounds for eviction or termination of tenancy, and no fines or fees could be charged for it.
Suspended rent could not be treated as tenant debt or reported to consumer reporting agencies, so credit scores would not be harmed.

The bill authorized whatever sums were necessary to reimburse assisted-housing owners and public housing agencies for lost rent and pandemic-related cost increases, including higher Section 8 housing assistance payments.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost through a new appropriation covering every dollar of suspended rent, plus any increase in landlords' operating costs and in housing assistance payments, with no dollar cap in the bill. Renters in unsubsidized private market housing—the majority of American renters—would get nothing from this bill.

drawbacks.text: The reimbursement authorization was open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary'), giving Congress no upfront cost estimate for a program covering rent in every federally assisted housing program nationwide.
The bill covered only federally assisted housing; tenants in ordinary private rental units, most renters during the pandemic, would have received no rent relief from it.

Because owners would be reimbursed 100% of suspended rent plus added costs, the bill transfers money through landlords rather than directly to tenants, guaranteeing owners no financial loss even as it relieves tenants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection—no rent owed, no eviction, no credit damage for subsidized-housing tenants during a pandemic—is substantial for the households covered, and the main cost (fully reimbursing owners) is a deliberate design choice that removes landlord opposition. The real limits are its open-ended cost to taxpayers and its narrow reach: it does nothing for the majority of renters in unassisted housing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velázquez introduced the bill on March 23, 2020, twelve days after the national COVID-19 emergency was declared.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken—the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, assisted-housing landlords kept collecting rent from tenants with no federal reimbursement alternative, and subsidized-housing tenants had to keep paying rent through the pandemic. The federal Treasury spent nothing, but renters got none of the promised relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Subsidized-housing landlords, whose tenants kept paying rent

for.name: Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend rent obligations in federally assisted housing during the COVID-19 emergency with full federal reimbursement to owners.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 23, 2020 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; sponsorship was Democratic (the sponsor plus 2 Democratic cosponsors), so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Owners of federally assisted housing (subsidized-housing landlords)
industries.note: The bill would have suspended tenant rent but reimbursed owners 100% of lost rent plus pandemic-related cost increases, so owners would lose nothing while their tenants got relief. In this bill the landlords' financial interest ran alongside tenants' relief because taxpayers covered the gap.
PHAs would have been reimbursed for lost tenant rent, for any increase in Section 8 housing assistance payments caused by the suspension, and for added administrative costs.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and consumer credit reporting
industries.note: The bill barred reporting suspended nonpayment of rent to consumer reporting agencies, cutting off a source of adverse tenant records these firms compile and sell.
